purpose: Demo data contract for the end-to-end analog chip readiness journey.
main_question: Can this workload run well on this analog chip, what proof do we have, what breaks, and what must be built or measured next?

steps.title: Model Intake
steps.intro: The user learns whether the platform can open the model and understand its basic shape. This starts the review from a real file instead of a slide claim.
steps.question: Can the platform read the model inputs, outputs, layers, operators, and size?
steps.evidence: Model parser output and package metadata. This is not proof that the chip can run the model.
steps.next: Run analog fit after the model structure is available.
steps.result: Demo result: the model structure is available, but chip fit is still unknown until analog fit and compiler mapping run.
steps.missing: Missing proof: no analog mapping, no simulator result, no compiler result, and no hardware result yet.

steps.title: Analog Fit
steps.intro: The user learns which model parts may be good candidates for analog compute and which parts should stay digital.
steps.question: Which layers are repeated matrix math, and which layers need digital logic or fallback?
steps.evidence: Analog candidate list, digital-required list, unsupported operator list, and analog/digital boundary.
steps.next: Run analog accuracy risk and crossbar layout checks for the candidate layers.
steps.result: Demo result: the platform can separate likely analog candidates from parts that need digital compute or rewrite.
steps.missing: Missing proof: this is a fit estimate until simulator, compiler, and board evidence confirm it.

steps.title: Analog Accuracy Risk
steps.intro: The user learns whether analog behavior may change the model answer enough to matter.
steps.question: Will noise, drift, limited precision, or imperfect weight writing hurt the output?
steps.evidence: AIHWKIT, local analog-error adapter, or related simulator output. This is simulation unless backed by hardware.
steps.next: Compare simulated accuracy risk with the task tolerance.
steps.result: Demo result: simulator evidence can show likely accuracy risk under stated analog assumptions.
steps.missing: Missing proof: simulator output does not prove board accuracy or production behavior.

steps.title: Crossbar Layout Risk
steps.intro: The user learns whether the physical memory grid may create errors after the model is placed on arrays.
steps.question: Do wire effects, bit slicing, read noise, programming error, or converter range create risk?
steps.evidence: CrossSim output or local crossbar layout estimates tied to the mapped layers.
steps.next: Use layout risk to update the hardware cost and compiler mapping.
steps.result: Demo result: layout evidence can show whether the memory grid may damage model accuracy.
steps.missing: Missing proof: crossbar simulation does not prove the final packaged chip or board.

steps.title: Hardware Cost Estimate
steps.intro: The user learns whether the workload is realistic for the chip budget.
steps.question: How much area, memory, energy, latency, and converter work does this workload need?
steps.evidence: NeuroSim, MNSIM, or local estimator output. This stays an estimate until measured.
steps.next: Use the cost estimate to decide whether the workload is a first target or later target.
steps.result: Demo result: the platform can estimate area, energy, latency, memory, and converter cost for planning.
steps.missing: Missing proof: estimates must stay labeled until silicon or board measurements exist.

steps.title: Compiler Mapping
steps.intro: The user learns whether normal model code can become a chip execution plan.
steps.question: Can the compiler place the model on analog tiles, digital logic, memory, and runtime commands?
steps.evidence: analog-mlir, local compiler estimate, or our future chip target report.
steps.next: Generate a simulation target now and a board-loadable package later.
steps.result: Demo result: compiler evidence can show what maps to analog, what stays digital, and what is blocked.
steps.missing: Missing proof: a simulation target is not the same as a board-loadable chip package.

steps.title: Transformer And VLA Check
steps.intro: The user learns which modern model parts are analog candidates and which parts should stay digital.
steps.question: Which static projection or feed-forward parts can use analog, and which attention, normalization, action, or safety parts stay digital?
steps.evidence: Transformer/VLA partition report with analog candidates, digital-required regions, and rewrite options.
steps.next: Block full-VLA analog claims unless mapping, runtime, and task evidence support them.
steps.result: Demo result: the platform can prevent a partial analog fit from becoming a false full-VLA claim.
steps.missing: Missing proof: full VLA readiness needs mapping, runtime, task, safety, and update evidence.

steps.title: Full-System Runtime
steps.intro: The user learns whether the surrounding system overhead may erase the analog benefit.
steps.question: Do CPU work, memory movement, dispatch, synchronization, ADCs, or DACs dominate runtime?
steps.evidence: SST/Golem, ALPINE/gem5-X, gem5, or local runtime estimator output.
steps.next: Use system timing to decide what must be scheduled, moved, or redesigned.
steps.result: Demo result: system evidence can show whether host, memory, or signal conversion overhead changes the story.
steps.missing: Missing proof: system simulation still needs board traces before measured latency claims.

steps.title: Board Runtime
steps.intro: The user learns whether the package actually ran on a prototype board or lab setup.
steps.question: Did the board load the package, start the run, finish the run, and report timing?
steps.evidence: Board trace with firmware version, board setup, pass/fail, latency, jitter, and failure reason.
steps.next: Tie the same run to power, thermal, and task accuracy evidence.
steps.result: Demo result: board runtime can support a measured latency claim for the exact setup tested.
steps.missing: Missing proof: board runtime alone does not prove energy savings or task accuracy.

steps.title: Power And Thermal
steps.intro: The user learns how much energy the run used and how hot the setup became.
steps.question: Was power measured for the whole board, the chip, or only one rail, and what temperature was reached?
steps.evidence: Power trace, energy per run, peak power, thermal trace, and measurement setup.
steps.next: Separate measured power from estimates and connect it to task accuracy.
steps.result: Demo result: power and thermal traces can support measured energy and heat claims.
steps.missing: Missing proof: the trace must match the same model package, board, firmware, and task run.

steps.title: Task Accuracy
steps.intro: The user learns whether the mapped or hardware-run model still solves the real task.
steps.question: Does the result match the baseline closely enough for the user's actual workload?
steps.evidence: Baseline metric, mapped-model metric, hardware-run metric when available, tolerance, and sample count.
steps.next: Use task accuracy to decide whether speed or power evidence is meaningful.
steps.result: Demo result: task accuracy shows whether the hardware path still solves the user's real problem.
steps.missing: Missing proof: speed and power are incomplete if the model no longer meets the task target.

steps.title: Weight Update Readiness
steps.intro: The user learns whether the chip can change model weights after deployment.
steps.question: Is the chip fixed-weight only, occasional-update capable, adapter-update capable, or adaptive blocked?
steps.evidence: Update scope, update frequency, write time, write energy, endurance, retention, rollback, and post-update accuracy.
steps.next: Block adaptive Physical AI claims until update evidence exists.
steps.result: Demo result: update evidence decides whether the chip supports fixed weights, rare updates, adapter updates, or adaptation.
steps.missing: Missing proof: adaptive claims need write cost, endurance, retention, rollback, and post-update accuracy.

steps.title: Sensor Boundary Readiness
steps.intro: The user learns what happens before the model input.
steps.question: Are sensor capture, preprocessing, buffering, synchronization, latency, and energy counted?
steps.evidence: Sensor path report for camera, event, tactile, audio, industrial, or other physical inputs.
steps.next: Tie sensor-to-answer cost to the final fit decision.
steps.result: Demo result: sensor-path evidence shows whether the chip claim includes the cost of getting real-world signals into the model.
steps.missing: Missing proof: chip-only results are incomplete if sensor capture and preprocessing are ignored.

steps.title: Final Answer
steps.intro: The user gets one direct answer that separates fit, proof, broken parts, safe claims, blocked claims, and next work.
steps.question: What can we safely say today, and what must be built or measured next?
steps.evidence: Combined evidence package from every completed step and every blocked step.
steps.next: Export the review package for executives, customers, investors, and engineering teams.
steps.result: Demo result: the final answer gives fit, proof, broken parts, safe claims, blocked claims, and next work.
steps.missing: Missing proof: any unverified claim stays blocked in the exported review package.
